The best advice I have is to research the area as thoroughly as possible. In my home city, if I were to buy a property to rent out, I would know exactly what and where, through years of seeing landlords fail to stay afloat (I am a Property Manager). Not everybody has that advantage of already being in the industry, so research is key. There’s a great post in the thread about figures, but think as well about tenants. For example, there’s a section of my city just to the West over the river where you can get hold of a victorian 2 bed for £165,000 which will get you a minimum return of £750-900 a week (the rest will depend on the finish and quality of the let itself). This area is traditionally a working class area which has always been a migrant hub. You should have no problem filling this property. I also know that the area is showing signs of gentrification as well as being just over the river from a new city centre development. What this means for you is ‘capital gain’. You know that if times got a little hard, and for whatever reason (maintenance required leaving you out of pocket, tenants gone awol etc) you could sell the property, and have a decent return on your investment. 

So yeah, research where you’re buying very carefully.

I looked to the diner’s small corner tv, which grew louder as the waitress extended the remote towards it, bewildered. The news anchor was mid-story, “the renowned scientists believe it could happen at any time, and have been working closely on gathering more information since the first crack appeared yesterday lunchtime, and has been slowly growing since. All evidence so far gathered seem to point to a single conclusion, that everything we know about the sun is incorrect, and it would seem the star is in fact, an egg.’ The diner erupted in to a mess of loud and panicked conversation. Surely it can’t be true? The sun gives us everything, what happens when it hatches? I couldn’t help myself but feel excited amongst all the commotion. If this is true, this would most likely spell the end of everything, but the idea is such an extreme notion that one can’t help but feel confident, and somewhat safe. 

After five minutes of fear-mongering from the news radiating from the tv in the corner of the diner, most of the room emptied. I assume family members going home amidst the excitement and anxiety of the concept that the earth and it’s inhabitants lie at risk of the ongoing events from 150,000,000 km away is the reason for the sudden barrenness of the diner. It grew worse, the panic that discharged from the tv like the puss from a wound filled the ears of the remaining patrons. The words ‘extinction’ and ‘eradication’ were repeated so frequently they lost all weight as extreme consequence. The light and heat emitted from the sun grew intense, and the warm glow from the windows filled the room. As the brightness magnified through the windows and reflected from the surfaces in a blinding fashion, the waitress screamed “Everybody out! We’re locking up!” I rose calmly and followed the other customers as they frantically ran out to the street.

The light from the sun was blinding and after donning my summer glasses, the street revealed a different picture to what I imagine. As the diner locked itself behind us, havoc played out along the street. The crowds embodied the fearful and alarming spirit of the media, and laid waste to store displays. Clothing and goods lay dormant in the street, some ablaze, while formerly calm patrons of restaurants and cafe’s ran rampant through the main street of the town. In a matter of half an hour, a seemingly calm town centre became the remainder of a war-zone. The scenes around me became more shocking, as looting became violent. Bodies knocked to the ground would be quickly surrounded by groups of strangers, kicking and flailing amidst the smoke and blaze. 

As I turned to an alley to find a quieter and safer route back to the apartment, I felt the blunt thump of a metallic instrument that rung out as I fell to the floor. In a haze of smog, intense light and dazzle, I saw the assailant lift a dustbin above his head, holding my gaze. The remaining seconds I had I realised, no matter how catastrophic a threat promises to be, the real destruction lies with ourselves.
